screens.heading: You are safe here
screens.reassurance: This module will not change your phone plan or contact your carrier. You are just reading.
screens.goal: By the end of this module, you will understand what your mobile plan includes, whether you are paying too much, and how to confidently negotiate a better deal with your carrier.

screens.heading: Why long-term customers usually overpay
body: Canadian mobile carriers — Rogers, Bell, Telus, Fido, Virgin, Koodo — regularly offer promotional rates to attract new customers. Long-term customers rarely receive these offers automatically. The result: loyal customers often pay $20-40 more per month than new customers for the same plan.
This is not because you did anything wrong. It is because carriers rely on inertia. Checking your plan once a year and asking for a better deal costs you nothing and frequently saves you money.
The first step: know what you currently have. Check your current plan by logging in to your carrier's app or website. Look for 'My Plan,' 'Account,' or 'Usage.'
screens.tellMeMore: The CRTC's Wireless Code gives you the right to cancel your mobile plan at any time after 24 months without a cancellation fee. If you signed up with a two-year contract, you can switch carriers freely once that period ends. This is your single most powerful negotiating tool: the ability to leave.

screens.heading: What do you actually use your phone for?
body: Most seniors use their phones for: calling family, texting, checking email, looking things up on the internet, and occasional video calls. This is a low-to-moderate data user profile.
Check your actual data usage: in your phone's Settings, look for 'Mobile Data' or 'Cellular.' It shows how much data each app has used this month. Most people are surprised by how little they use.
If you are consistently using under 2 GB of data per month, you may not need the 5 GB or 10 GB plan you are paying for. A smaller plan could save you $15-30 per month.
screens.tellMeMore: Most of the data-heavy activities — streaming Netflix, watching YouTube, making video calls — happen over Wi-Fi at home, which does not count against your mobile data. Mobile data is only used when you are away from home Wi-Fi: browsing on the bus, looking up directions on a walk, checking messages at a restaurant.

screens.heading: Getting a better deal
body: Call your carrier and say: 'I have been a customer for [X] years. I am seeing better deals for new customers. I would like to know what you can offer me to stay.' This works more often than people expect.

Budget carriers (Fido, Koodo, Virgin, Public Mobile, Chatr, Lucky Mobile) often offer the same network coverage at 30-50% lower prices — they use the same towers as their parent companies (Rogers, Telus, Bell).
If your current carrier will not match a competitor's price, you can switch. Number porting (keeping your existing phone number when you move to a new carrier) is free and takes effect the same day.
screens.tellMeMore: Canada has some of the highest mobile rates in the world — but the CRTC has been pushing carriers to offer $50 or less for plans with at least 5 GB of data. Ask specifically: 'Do you have any plans at $50 or under?' Many carriers now have these available but do not advertise them prominently. They are sometimes called 'accessible plans' or 'core plans.'

screens.heading: Roaming and travel
body: Using your phone in another country without a roaming plan can result in very large bills — sometimes hundreds of dollars for a short trip.

Before travelling internationally: call your carrier and ask about a travel add-on. Most carriers offer temporary roaming packages ($10-15 per day for unlimited data and calls) that are much less expensive than accidental roaming charges.
Alternatively: put your phone in Airplane Mode when abroad and use only Wi-Fi. Or purchase a local SIM card at your destination — many airports sell them for $20-30 and include local calls and data.
screens.tellMeMore: Within Canada, there is no roaming — your Canadian plan works the same in British Columbia as it does in Ontario. You will not be charged extra for calling or texting someone in another province, and your data cap applies across the entire country. If you see 'Extended Coverage' on your phone, you are in a rural area using a partner network — this is normal and included in your plan.

screens.heading: You are paying for a service — make sure you are getting a fair price
takeaways: Check your actual monthly data usage in Settings — you may be on a plan much bigger than you need.
Long-term customers routinely overpay. Call your carrier annually and ask for their best current offer.
Budget carriers (Fido, Koodo, Virgin) use the same towers as major carriers at lower prices.
Number porting is free — you can take your phone number when you switch carriers.
Always add a roaming package before travelling internationally. Accidental roaming is very expensive.
screens.confidence: You now understand your mobile plan well enough to know if you are getting fair value — and exactly what to say to get a better deal.
